questions.stem: Which of the followings is false about C.perfringens ?

options.label: A
options.text: Food poisoning strains produce heat resistant spores

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Most important toxin is hyaluronidase. The most important toxin of Clostridium perfringens is Alpha toxin a lecithinase (phospholipase C) that disrupts cell membranes by hydrolyzing lecithin, leading to cell lysis, tissue destruction, and contributing to gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis). This toxin plays a crucial role in the virulence of C. perfringens, causing hemolysis, increased vascular permeability, and necrosis. While hyaluronidase is present as a spreading factor, it is not the most significant toxin. Incorrect Options: (A) Food poisoning strains produce heat-resistant spores Clostridium perfringens type A, which causes food poisoning, produces heat-resistant spores that can survive cooking temperatures. These spores germinate when food is kept at warm temperatures (between 40–60°C), leading to bacterial proliferation and toxin production in the intestines, causing watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps. (B) Show positive Nagler reaction The Nagler reaction is used to detect lecithinase (alpha-toxin) activity on egg yolk agar. C. perfringens gives a positive Nagler reaction, seen as opacification around the colonies, due to the breakdown of lecithin in the medium. This reaction is a diagnostic test for C. perfringens. (D) Most common cause of gas gangrene C. perfringens is the most common cause of gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis), a rapidly spreading soft tissue infection characterized by crepitus (gas in tissues), severe pain, foul-smelling discharge, and tissue necrosis. It results from deep wound infections, particularly in traumatic or surgical wounds contaminated with soil or feces. The alpha-toxin and other degradative enzymes promote tissue destruction and spread of infection.

questions.stem: All are true regarding tetanus except

options.label: A
options.text: Transmission through contaminated wounds and injuries

options.label: B
options.text: More common in winters and dry weather

options.label: C
options.text: Reservoir in soil and intestines of humans and animals

options.label: D
options.text: No herd immunity or lifelong immunity

questions.answerText: More common in winters and dry weather
questions.solutionHtml: tion of Other Options: (A) Transmission through contaminated wounds and injuries – (Correct) Tetanus is transmitted through spores of Clostridium tetani, which enter the body via contaminated wounds, deep puncture injuries, burns, surgical wounds, umbilical stump (neonatal tetanus), and injecting drug use. The spores germinate under anaerobic conditions and produce tetanospasmin, a potent neurotoxin causing muscle rigidity and spasms. (C) Reservoir in soil and intestines of humans and animals – (Correct) Clostridium tetani is found in soil, dust, and the intestines of humans and animals (especially herbivores like cattle and horses). The bacterium produces highly resistant spores that can remain viable for years in the environment, making it a constant potential source of infection. (D) No herd immunity or lifelong immunity – (Correct) Unlike many infections, tetanus does not induce natural immunity after infection because the amount of toxin required to cause disease is too small to stimulate an immune response. This is why individuals who recover from tetanus still require vaccination. Additionally, since C. tetani is an environmental pathogen, herd immunity does not protect against tetanus, and regular booster doses of the tetanus vaccine (TT/Td) are necessary for lifelong protection.

questions.stem: Most common cause of antibiotic induced colitis
questions.solutionHtml: n of Other Options: (A) Escherichia coli – (Incorrect) Although Escherichia coli (such as Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) and Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC)) can cause infectious diarrhea, it is not associated with antibiotic-induced colitis. E. coli infections are usually due to contaminated food or water rather than antibiotic use. (C) Salmonella – (Incorrect) Salmonella species cause gastroenteritis (non-typhoidal Salmonella) and typhoid fever (Salmonella Typhi/Paratyphi), but they do not cause antibiotic-associated colitis. In fact, antibiotics are usually avoided in uncomplicated Salmonella gastroenteritis, as they can prolong the carrier state. (D) Campylobacter jejuni – (Incorrect) Campylobacter jejuni is a common cause of bacterial gastroenteritis, often from undercooked poultry or contaminated water. It can cause bloody diarrhea and post-infectious complications like Guillain-Barré syndrome, but it is not the leading cause of antibiotic-associated colitis.

questions.stem: Each of the following statements concerning Clostridium perfringens is correct except

options.label: C
options.text: It produces an exotoxin that degrades lecithin and causes necrosis and hemolysis

options.label: D
options.text: It is a gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose

questions.answerText: It is a gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose
questions.solutionHtml: n of Correct Statements: (A) It causes gas gangrene – (Correct) Clostridium perfringens is a well-known cause of gas gangrene, also known as clostridial myonecrosis. This condition occurs when the bacteria infects deep tissues, usually following trauma or surgery. The bacteria release powerful exotoxins that cause extensive tissue necrosis and gas formation, leading to the characteristic swollen, foul-smelling, and necrotic tissue in affected areas. (B) It causes food poisoning – (Correct) Clostridium perfringens is a common cause of food poisoning. The bacterium produces heat-labile enterotoxins that can cause symptoms like abdominal cramping and diarrhea. This typically occurs after consuming contaminated meat or poultry that has been inadequately cooked or stored, allowing the bacteria to multiply and produce toxins. (C) It produces an exotoxin that degrades lecithin and causes necrosis and hemolysis – (Correct) Clostridium perfringens produces several exotoxins, including alpha-toxin, which is a lecithinase (phospholipase C). This toxin breaks down lecithin, a component of cell membranes, leading to cell lysis, tissue necrosis, and hemolysis. This mechanism is a key factor in the tissue destruction seen in gas gangrene.

questions.stem: Boxcar appearance is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Streptococci: Streptococci are gram-positive cocci that typically arrange themselves in chains or pairs. They do not have a boxcar appearance since they are round (cocci) rather than rod-shaped. (C) Toxoplasma: Toxoplasma gondii is a protozoan parasite that does not exhibit a boxcar morphology. Instead, it has a crescent or banana shape in its tachyzoite form and appears as tissue cysts in chronic infections. It is the causative agent of toxoplasmosis, which can be particularly severe in pregnant women and immunocompromised patients. (D) Treponema pallidum: Treponema pallidum is a spirochete, meaning it has a thin, helical, corkscrew shape rather than a boxcar-like rectangular shape. It is the causative agent of syphilis and is typically identified using dark-field microscopy or serological tests rather than conventional Gram staining.

questions.stem: Nagler reaction is shown by:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Clostridium difficile: C. difficile does not produce alpha toxin or lecithinase, making it Nagler-negative. It is primarily known for producing toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin), which are responsible for pseudomembranous colitis. (C) Clostridium tetani: C. tetani is Nagler-negative because it does not produce lecithinase. Instead, it produces tetanospasmin, a neurotoxin responsible for spastic paralysis (tetanus). (D) Clostridium butyricum: C. butyricum does not produce lecithinase and is Nagler-negative. It is mostly known for its ability to produce butyric acid during fermentation rather than producing significant toxins.

questions.stem: Mechanism of action of Tetanospasmin:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Inhibition of cAMP: Tetanospasmin does not act by inhibiting cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). In contrast, some bacterial toxins, such as cholera toxin and pertussis toxin, increase cAMP levels, leading to cellular dysfunction and diarrhea. This mechanism is unrelated to tetanospasmin. (C) Inactivation of ACh receptors: Tetanospasmin does not inactivate acetylcholine (ACh) receptors. Instead, it prevents the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters. Clostridium botulinum produces botulinum toxin, which blocks ACh release at neuromuscular junctions, leading to flaccid paralysis, which is the opposite of tetanus. (D) Inhibition of cGMP: Tetanospasmin has no effect on cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) pathways. cGMP is involved in vascular smooth muscle relaxation, and its inhibition is more relevant to toxins like heat-stable enterotoxin of Escherichia coli (ST toxin), which affects intestinal secretion.

questions.stem: Cause of Clostridiumdifficile associated diarrhea.
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Trauma: Trauma itself does not cause C. difficile–associated diarrhea. However, hospitalization, prolonged bed rest, and surgeries can increase the risk by necessitating antibiotic use, which leads to C. difficile overgrowth. But trauma alone is not a direct cause, making this option incorrect. (B) Dairy products: Consumption of dairy products does not cause C. difficile diarrhea. While probiotics (found in some dairy products like yogurt) may help prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea, dairy itself is not a risk factor for C. difficile infection. (C) Fried rice: Fried rice is associated with Bacillus cereus food poisoning, which causes vomiting or diarrheal illness but not C. difficile infection. This makes option (C) incorrect.

questions.stem: Positive Schick's test indicates that person is:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Immune to diphtheria: A negative Schick test (no skin reaction) indicates immunity because the person has pre-existing antibodies that neutralize the diphtheria toxin. Since a positive Schick test indicates susceptibility rather than immunity, this option is incorrect. (B) Hypersensitive to diphtheria: A hypersensitive reaction to diphtheria toxin would result in an exaggerated immediate allergic response, which is not the basis of the Schick test. The test only determines antibody presence or absence, not hypersensitivity, making this option incorrect. (D) Carrier of diphtheria: A carrier of Corynebacterium diphtheriae harbors the bacteria without showing symptoms but may or may not have antibodies. The Schick test does not determine carrier status; it only assesses susceptibility to infection, so this option is incorrect.

questions.stem: Literally leather term is used for:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Anthrax: Anthrax, caused by Bacillus anthracis, is associated with black eschar formation in cutaneous anthrax, but this does not resemble leathery pseudomembrane formation seen in diphtheria. Pulmonary and gastrointestinal anthrax have different clinical presentations, making this option incorrect. (B) Proteus: Proteus species are motile, urease-positive gram-negative rods known for their swarming motility on agar. They are primarily associated with urinary tract infections and do not produce a leathery pseudomembrane. (D) Neisseria: Neisseria species, including Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, are gram-negative diplococci that cause meningitis and sexually transmitted infections, respectively. They do not form pseudomembranes or have any leathery tissue characteristics.

questions.stem: True about diphtheria is:

options.label: A
options.text: Cause cranial nerve palsies in 2nd and 3rd week

options.label: D
options.text: Passive immunization is harmful and should not be tried

questions.answerText: Cause cranial nerve palsies in 2nd and 3rd week
questions.solutionHtml: n of Incorrect Options: (B) Treatment with erythromycin – Incorrect While erythromycin is one of the antibiotics used to eliminate C. diphtheriae, the primary treatment of diphtheria is early administration of diphtheria antitoxin to neutralize circulating toxin. Penicillin G or erythromycin is used to eradicate the bacteria and prevent further toxin production, but antibiotics alone do not neutralize the pre-formed toxin, making this option incomplete. (C) It is a gram-negative organism – Incorrect Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a gram-positive club-shaped bacillus that appears in Chinese letter arrangements under the microscope. It is a non-spore-forming, non-motile facultative anaerobe, making this statement incorrect. (D) Passive immunization is harmful and should not be tried – Incorrect Passive immunization with diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) is the mainstay of treatment and should be given as early as possible to neutralize circulating toxin before it binds to tissues. Delayed administration increases the risk of complications, including myocarditis and neuropathy. While serum sickness can occur as a side effect, it is not harmful if managed properly, and the benefits outweigh the risks.

questions.stem: Toxigenicity of C. diphtheria is determined by:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Ascoli’s Reaction – Incorrect Ascoli’s reaction is a thermoprecipitation test used for detecting anthrax antigen in tissue samples. It is primarily used to identify Bacillus anthracis in suspected cases of anthrax and has no role in diagnosing diphtheria or determining the toxigenicity of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. (C) Nagler’s Reaction – Incorrect Nagler’s reaction is used to detect alpha-toxin (lecithinase activity) of Clostridium perfringens. It involves the opacification of egg yolk agar due to the enzymatic breakdown of lecithin. This test is specific for Clostridium perfringens and is not related to diphtheria toxigenicity testing. (D) All – Incorrect Since only Elek’s gel precipitation test (A) is specific for detecting diphtheria toxin, option D (All) is incorrect. Neither Ascoli’s reaction nor Nagler’s reaction plays a role in determining the toxigenicity of Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

questions.stem: Investigation of choice of diphtheria carrier is:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Gram's Stain – Incorrect Gram staining can reveal Gram-positive, club-shaped bacilli arranged in Chinese letter or palisade patterns, which are characteristic of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. However, it does not differentiate between toxigenic and non-toxigenic strains, nor does it confirm the presence of viable bacteria. It is useful for preliminary diagnosis but not the investigation of choice for carriers. (C) Albert's Stain – Incorrect Albert's stain is a special stain used to detect metachromatic granules (Babes-Ernst granules) in C. diphtheriae. These granules appear as dark blue or bluish-black structures in a green cytoplasm, helping to identify the organism. However, like Gram’s stain, it is only a screening tool and does not confirm active colonization or carrier status, making it inferior to culture. (D) Ziehl-Neelsen Stain – Incorrect Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain is used for acid-fast bacteria (AFB) detection, particularly Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Since Corynebacterium diphtheriae is not acid-fast, this stain has no role in its identification, making it an incorrect choice.

questions.stem: Selective medium for Corynebacterium diptheriae is:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Loeffler’s Serum – Incorrect Loeffler’s serum medium is an enrichment medium, not a selective medium. It enhances the growth of C. diphtheriae by promoting the formation of metachromatic granules but does not inhibit other bacteria. It is useful for rapid preliminary identification but not ideal for selective isolation. (B) MacConkey’s Medium – Incorrect MacConkey’s agar is selective for Gram-negative bacteria, particularly enteric bacteria, due to the presence of bile salts and crystal violet. Since C. diphtheriae is a Gram-positive bacillus, it does not grow on MacConkey’s agar, making it unsuitable for its isolation. (D) Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) Medium – Incorrect LJ medium is a specialized medium for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, containing malachite green, which inhibits non-mycobacterial flora. Corynebacterium diphtheriae does not grow on LJ medium, making it an incorrect choice.

questions.stem: C. diphtheriae is also called as:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Koch’s Bacillus – Incorrect Koch’s bacillus refers to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis. It was discovered by Robert Koch in 1882. Since C. diphtheriae is unrelated to tuberculosis, this option is incorrect. (B) Roux Bacillus – Incorrect Pierre Roux, a French bacteriologist, contributed to diphtheria research, particularly in toxin production and vaccine development, but C. diphtheriae is not named after him. The term "Roux bacillus" is not associated with any specific bacterium. (D) Yersin Bacillus – Incorrect Yersinia pestis, the bacterium responsible for plague, is sometimes referred to as Yersin’s bacillus, named after Alexandre Yersin, who discovered it in 1894. Since C. diphtheriae is not related to plague, this option is incorrect.

questions.stem: Reverse CAMP test is positive for
questions.solutionHtml: ion for the Correct Answer: Clostridium perfringens is positive for the reverse CAMP test, which is used to differentiate it from other Clostridium species. The reverse CAMP test is based on the interaction between the alpha toxin of C. perfringens and the *beta-hemolysin of Staphylococcus aureus. In this test, C. perfringens is streaked perpendicular to Staphylococcus aureus on a blood agar plate. If C. perfringens is present, it enhances hemolysis, forming an arrowhead-shaped zone of hemolysis at the intersection of both streaks. This reaction is opposite to the CAMP test, which is used to identify Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus). Explanation for Incorrect Options: (A) Clostridium tetani – Incorrect. C. tetani is a strict anaerobe that causes tetanus due to its neurotoxin (tetanospasmin), but it does not produce an alpha toxin like C. perfringens. It does not give a reverse CAMP test positive reaction. (C) Clostridium difficile – Incorrect. C. difficile is primarily known for its toxin-mediated pseudomembranous colitis and is detected using toxin assays (Toxin A and Toxin B) rather than the reverse CAMP test. It does not produce alpha toxin like C. perfringens, so it is negative in the reverse CAMP test. (D) Clostridium novyi – Incorrect. C. novyi is known for producing gas gangrene in infections but does not give a positive reverse CAMP test. It primarily produces toxins (alpha and beta toxins), but their mechanism does not interact with S. aureus beta-hemolysin. (E) Clostridium septicum – Incorrect. C. septicum is associated with spontaneous gas gangrene, especially in patients with colon cancer or immunosuppression. It produces toxins but does not exhibit a reverse CAMP test positive reaction.

questions.stem: 7 month-old infant presents with failure to thrive, progressive muscular weakness, and poor head control. On questioning, the mother states that she typically feeds the baby soy-based formula sweetened with honey. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be responsible for the child's presentation?
questions.solutionHtml: ion for the Correct Answer: The infant's failure to thrive, progressive muscular weakness, and poor head control are classic symptoms of infant botulism, which is caused by Clostridium botulinum. This condition occurs when C. botulinum spores are ingested (commonly from honey), germinate in the immature gut, and produce botulinum toxin. Key features of infant botulism: Floppy baby syndrome – hypotonia, poor feeding, weak cry. Descending paralysis – starting from cranial nerves (poor head control, ptosis, weak suck). Autonomic dysfunction – constipation (often the first sign), poor reflexes. History of honey consumption – a known risk factor due to C. botulinum spores present in honey. Since the infant in the case was fed a honey-sweetened soy-based formula, this is a strong clue pointing toward C. botulinum, making option (A) the correct answer. Explanation for Incorrect Options: (B) Clostridium difficile – Incorrect C. difficile is associated with antibiotic-associated colitis, primarily affecting hospitalized or antibiotic-treated patients. It causes diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis, not progressive muscle weakness or flaccid paralysis. (C) Clostridium perfringens – Incorrect This organism is mainly associated with gas gangrene (myonecrosis) and food poisoning (watery diarrhea), but not neuromuscular weakness. It does not cause floppy baby syndrome. (D) Clostridium tetani – Incorrect C. tetani produces tetanospasmin toxin, which causes spastic paralysis (rigidity, muscle spasms, lockjaw) rather than the flaccid paralysis seen in botulism. Unlike C. botulinum, which blocks acetylcholine release, C. tetani blocks inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA & glycine), leading to uncontrolled muscle contraction instead of weakness.

questions.stem: All cause Fournier gangrene except
questions.solutionHtml: ion for the Correct Answer: Clostridium species, particularly Clostridium perfringens, are known to cause gas gangrene (myonecrosis) but not typically Fournier gangrene. Fournier gangrene is a necrotizing fasciitis of the perineal, genital, and perianal regions, primarily caused by facultative and anaerobic bacteria in a synergistic polymicrobial infection. While Clostridium species can contribute to deep soft tissue infections, they are not a primary causative agent of Fournier gangrene. Explanation for the Incorrect Options: (A) Staphylococcus – Incorrect Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) have been identified in polymicrobial infections leading to Fournier gangrene. They contribute by producing toxins and enzymes (e.g., hyaluronidase, coagulase) that enhance tissue destruction. (B) Streptococcus – Incorrect Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) is a common cause of necrotizing fasciitis, including Fournier gangrene. It produces exotoxins that lead to rapid tissue destruction, septic shock, and multi-organ failure. (D) Bacteroides – Incorrect Bacteroides species are anaerobic Gram-negative rods that are part of the normal gut flora and commonly contribute to polymicrobial infections in Fournier gangrene. They produce proteases and lipases, which facilitate tissue necrosis.

questions.stem: Gastrointestinal enteritis necroticans caused by
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Clostridium difficile: C. difficile causes antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis, not enteritis necroticans. It produces toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin), leading to inflammation and diarrhea, but it does not cause the extensive necrosis seen in enteritis necroticans. (C) Clostridium botulinum: C. botulinum is known for causing botulism, a neuroparalytic illness due to botulinum toxin, which blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions. It does not cause intestinal necrosis or enteritis necroticans. (D) Campylobacter jejuni: C. jejuni is a leading cause of bacterial gastroenteritis worldwide, but it typically causes self-limiting watery or bloody diarrhea rather than necrotizing enteritis. It is also associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome, but not enteritis necroticans. (E) Pseudomonas: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic pathogen responsible for hospital-acquired infections, including pneumonia, sepsis, and wound infections, but it does not cause enteritis necroticans.

questions.stem: Which species of Clostridium does not cause gangrene?
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Clostridium perfringens: C. perfringens is the most common cause of gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) due to its alpha toxin (phospholipase C), theta toxin, and other extracellular enzymes, which lead to rapid tissue destruction, gas production, and septic shock. It is the primary agent of traumatic gas gangrene. (B) Clostridium histolyticum: C. histolyticum produces collagenase and proteases, which contribute to tissue destruction and spread of gas gangrene. It is one of the less common causes of gas gangrene but is still involved in some polymicrobial clostridial infections. (C) Clostridium novyi: C. novyi (especially type A) can cause gas gangrene, similar to C. perfringens. It produces lethal toxins, including alpha toxin, leading to extensive tissue necrosis and gas formation. It is also linked to injection drug use-related clostridial infections.

questions.stem: The most effective way of preventing tetanus is:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Surgical debridement and toilet: Surgical wound cleaning and debridement help reduce bacterial load and remove necrotic tissue where C. tetani thrives. However, it does not neutralize the tetanus toxin, making it an important supportive but not the most effective preventive measure. (B) Hyperbaric oxygen: Clostridium tetani is an obligate anaerobe, meaning hyperbaric oxygen therapy (which increases oxygen concentration) can inhibit its growth. However, by the time symptoms appear, the toxin has already been released, and oxygen therapy does not neutralize tetanospasmin. It may help in wound management but is not a primary preventive measure. (C) Antibiotics: Antibiotics such as metronidazole or penicillin can kill C. tetani, reducing bacterial multiplication. However, they do not neutralize the toxin, meaning tetanus can still develop even after bacterial eradication. Active immunization is required for long-term prevention.

questions.stem: A patient of acute lymphocytic leukemia with fever and neutropenia develops diarrhea after administration of amoxicillin therapy, which of the following organisms is most likely to be the causative agent?
questions.solutionHtml: f Incorrect Options: (A) Salmonella typhi: S. typhi causes typhoid fever, which presents with step-ladder fever, abdominal pain, constipation (more common than diarrhea), and "pea soup" diarrhea in later stages. However, it is not typically associated with antibiotic use or neutropenia, making it an unlikely cause in this case. (C) Clostridium perfringens: C. perfringens causes foodborne gastroenteritis due to ingestion of contaminated meat, leading to watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps. However, it is not linked to antibiotic-associated diarrhea and does not cause pseudomembranous colitis like C. difficile. (D) Shigella flexneri: Shigella flexneri causes bacillary dysentery, characterized by bloody diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramps due to Shiga toxin production. However, it is not associated with antibiotic use, and its transmission occurs via fecal-oral contamination, which is less likely in a hospitalized neutropenic patient.

questions.stem: Sub terminal spores are found in:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Clostridium bifermentans: C. bifermentans is an anaerobic, spore-forming bacterium but does not consistently form subterminal spores. It is found in soil and human microbiota and is less commonly associated with infections. It does not exhibit the same toxigenic potential as C. perfringens. (C) Clostridium tetani: C. tetani is known for producing terminal spores, giving the bacteria its characteristic "drumstick" or "tennis racket" appearance. These highly resistant spores play a key role in its survival and transmission. Since C. tetani forms terminal spores, it is not the correct answer. (D) Clostridium tertium: C. tertium produces central or subterminal spores, but it is an aerotolerant species and is often a contaminant in clinical samples rather than a primary pathogen. While it can sporulate, it is not classically associated with subterminal spores like C. perfringens.

questions.stem: Clostridium group causes all except:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Diarrhea: Several Clostridium species, particularly Clostridium difficile, cause antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis due to the production of toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin). Additionally, Clostridium perfringens can cause foodborne diarrhea via its enterotoxin. Thus, Clostridium species are well-documented causes of diarrhea. (C) Local Necrosis: Clostridium perfringens and Clostridium histolyticum produce necrotizing toxins, leading to local tissue destruction, particularly in gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis). The alpha toxin (lecithinase) of C. perfringens is especially known for causing muscle necrosis and gas formation in infected tissues. (D) Antibiotic-Associated Changes: Clostridium difficile is the leading cause of antibiotic-associated colitis. Broad-spectrum antibiotic use disrupts the normal gut microbiota, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and produce toxins, leading to diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis.

questions.stem: Among the toxins produced by C.botulinum, the non- neurotoxic one is:
questions.solutionHtml: Incorrect Options: (A) A: Botulinum toxin type A is the most potent neurotoxin produced by C. botulinum. It is widely known for its clinical and cosmetic uses (e.g., Botox) as well as its role in foodborne botulism. It blocks acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis. (B) B: Botulinum toxin type B is another potent neurotoxin that inhibits acetylcholine release. It is used medically to treat muscle disorders and is also a cause of botulism. (C) C1: Botulinum toxin type C1 is a neurotoxin responsible for avian botulism and can affect other animals. It blocks neurotransmitter release, similar to other neurotoxic types. (E) D: Botulinum toxin type D is a neurotoxin that primarily affects cattle and birds. Like other neurotoxic types, it inhibits acetylcholine release, leading to paralysis.

questions.stem: Which type of Clostridium tetani has no flagella?
questions.solutionHtml: f Incorrect Options: (A) Type 1: Type 1 C. tetani possesses peritrichous flagella, meaning flagella are distributed all over its surface, making it motile. It does not fit the criteria of a non-flagellated strain. (B) Type 2: Similar to Type 1, Type 2 also has flagella and exhibits motility. It plays a role in tetanus pathogenesis but is not the non-motile variant. (C) Type 4: Type 4 C. tetani is also a motile strain, possessing peritrichous flagella like most other types. It does not meet the requirement for a non-flagellated strain.

questions.stem: Oval bulging terminal spores seen in:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Clostridium welchii (former name for Clostridium perfringens): C. welchii (now known as C. perfringens) does not form terminal spores. Instead, it produces subterminal spores, though sporulation is rare in clinical settings. It is primarily known for causing gas gangrene, food poisoning, and enteritis necroticans. (C) Clostridium perfringens: Like C. welchii, C. perfringens also produces subterminal spores, but they are rarely seen in laboratory cultures. This species is non-motile and responsible for gas gangrene and foodborne illnesses due to its potent toxins. Since it does not produce terminal spores, it is not the correct answer. (D) Clostridium histolyticum: C. histolyticum is a necrotizing species known for producing collagenases that degrade connective tissue. However, it forms subterminal spores, not terminal ones, and is associated with severe soft tissue infections.

questions.stem: Non-motile Clostridia is:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Clostridium novyi: C. novyi is a motile species due to the presence of flagella. It is primarily known for causing gas gangrene and is divided into two types (A and B), with Type A producing a potent alpha toxin that contributes to necrotic infections. Since it is motile, it is not the correct answer. (C) Clostridium botulinum: C. botulinum is also motile because it possesses peritrichous flagella. It is best known for producing botulinum toxin, which blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions, leading to flaccid paralysis in botulism. Since it exhibits motility, it is incorrect. (D) Clostridium difficile: C. difficile is motile due to the presence of flagella. It is responsible for antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis, caused by the toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin). Given its motility, it is not the correct answer.

questions.stem: Most common organism responsible for gas gangrene is:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Clostridium difficile: C. difficile is primarily associated with antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis, not gas gangrene. It produces toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin), which damage the intestinal lining, leading to severe colitis. Since it does not cause gas gangrene, it is an incorrect answer. (C) Clostridium tetani: C. tetani is the causative agent of tetanus, not gas gangrene. It produces tetanospasmin, a neurotoxin that blocks inhibitory neurotransmitters, leading to spastic paralysis and muscle rigidity. While C. tetani is an anaerobic, spore-forming bacillus like C. perfringens, it does not produce the tissue-destroying toxins necessary for gas gangrene. Thus, this is an incorrect option. (D) Clostridium botulinum: C. botulinum is responsible for botulism, a disease characterized by flaccid paralysis due to its production of botulinum toxin, which inhibits acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions. It does not cause soft tissue infections or gas gangrene, making this an incorrect choice.

questions.stem: All occur in botulism except
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Diarrhea. Clostridium botulinum produces botulinum toxin, which blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, leading to flaccid paralysis. The primary clinical features of botulism include descending paralysis, cranial nerve involvement, and autonomic dysfunction, but gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea are uncommon. Instead, botulism is often associated with constipation due to the inhibition of autonomic nerve function. Botulism can occur in different forms: Foodborne botulism (due to ingestion of preformed toxin in improperly canned foods) Infant botulism (due to ingestion of spores, often from honey, which colonize the intestine and produce toxin) Wound botulism (from spores infecting wounds and producing toxin in vivo) Iatrogenic botulism (from excessive botulinum toxin use in medical or cosmetic procedures) Incorrect Options: (A) Diplopia (Double Vision) – Incorrect. Botulinum toxin causes cranial nerve dysfunction, leading to blurred vision and diplopia due to paralysis of extraocular muscles. This is a classic early symptom of botulism. (C) Dysphagia (Difficulty Swallowing) – Incorrect. Botulinum toxin affects bulbar muscles, leading to dysphagia, which can cause choking and aspiration pneumonia. This is a key symptom of botulism. (D) Dysarthria (Difficulty Speaking) – Incorrect. The toxin-induced neuromuscular blockade affects the muscles responsible for speech, leading to dysarthria and a weak voice.

questions.stem: After leaving which of the following patients’ room would the use of alcohol-based hand rub be inadequate?

options.label: A
options.text: A 54-year-old man with quadriplegia admitted with a urinary tract infection caused by extended-spectrum β-lactamase–producing bacteria

options.label: B
options.text: A 78-year-old nursing home resident with recent antibiotic use and Clostridium difficile infection

options.label: C
options.text: A 35-year-old woman with advanced HIV infection and cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis

options.label: D
options.text: A 20-year-old renal transplant recipient with varicella pneumonia

questions.answerText: A 78-year-old nursing home resident with recent antibiotic use and Clostridium difficile infection
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Nosocomial infections have reservoirs and sources just as do community-acquired pathogens. In hospitalized patients, cross-contamination (i.e., indirect spread of organisms from one patient to the next) accounts for many nosocomial infections. Although hand hygiene is uniformly recommended for health care practitioners, adherence to hand washing is low often because of time pressure, inconvenience, and skin damage. Because of improved adherence, alcohol-based hand rubs are now recommended for all heath care workers except when hands are visibly soiled or after care of a patient with Clostridium difficile infection, whose spores may not be killed by alcohol and thus require thorough hand wash with soap and water.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with a long history of heroin abuse is brought to the hospital because of fever and worsening muscle spasms and pain over the past day. Because of long-standing venous sclerosis, he no longer injects intravenously but “skin pops,” often with dirty needles. On examination, he is extremely sweaty and febrile to 101.4°F. There are widespread muscle spasms, including the face. He is unable to open his jaw because of muscle spasm and has severe back pain because of diffuse spasm. On his leg, there is a skin wound that is tender and erythematous. All of the following statements regarding this patient are true EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Culture of the wound may reveal Clostridium tetani

options.label: B
options.text: Intrathecal antitoxin administration is recommended therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Permanent muscle dysfunction is likely after recovery.

questions.answerText: Permanent muscle dysfunction is likely after recovery.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Tetanus is an acute disease manifested by skeletal muscle spasm and autonomic nervous system disturbance. It is caused by a powerful neurotoxin produced by the bacterium Clostridium tetani and is now a rare disease because of widespread vaccination. There were fewer than 50 cases reported recently in the United States, but there is a rising frequency in drug users. Older patients may be at higher risk because of waning immunity. The differential diagnosis of a patient presenting with tetanus includes strychnine poisoning and drug-related dystonic reactions. The diagnosis is clinical. Cardiovascular instability is common because of autonomic dysfunction and is manifest by rapid fluctuation in heart rate and blood pressure. Wound culture results are positive in approximately 20% of cases. Metronidazole or penicillin should be administered to clear infection. Tetanus immune globulin is recommended over equine antiserum because of a lower risk of anaphylactic reactions. Recent evidence suggests that intrathecal administration is efficacious in inhibiting disease progression and improving outcomes. Muscle spasms may be treated with sedative drugs. With effective supportive care and often respiratory support, muscle function recovers after clearing the toxin with no residual damage.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. He recalls no unusual meals, sick contacts, or travel. He is hydrated with IV fluid, given antiemetics, and discharged home after feeling much better. Three days later, two of three blood cultures are positive for Clostridium perfringens. He is called at home and says that he feels fine and is back at work. What should your next instruction to the patient be?

options.label: B
options.text: Return for IV penicillin therapy plus echocardiography

options.label: C
options.text: Return for IV penicillin therapy plus colonoscopy.

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Clostridia are gram-positive, spore-forming obligate anaerobes that reside normally in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Several clostridial species can cause severe disease. Clostridium perfringens, which is the second most common clostridial species to normally colonize the GI tract, is associated with food poisoning, gas gangrene, and myonecrosis. C. septicum is seen often in conjunction with GI tumors. C. sordellii is associated with septic abortions. All can cause a fulminant overwhelming bacteremia, but this condition is rare. The fact that this patient is well several days after his acute complaints rules out this fulminant course. A more common scenario is transient, self-limited bacteremia caused by transient gut translocation during an episode of gastroenteritis. There is no need to treat when this occurs, and no further workup is necessary. Clostridium spp. sepsis rarely causes endocarditis because overwhelming disseminated intravascular coagulation and death occur so rapidly. Screening for GI tumor is warranted when C. septicum is cultured from the blood or a deep wound infection.

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old female presents to the casualty with presumed cellulitis on her left lower leg after getting a splinter in her foot, she is a known case of diabetes non compliant to medications. Her heel has a bluish hematoma with significant medial erythema. Laboratory result on peripheral blood demonstrated an elevated WBC count of 23,400/mm3 (normal, 4000 to 12,000/mL) with a left shift. Radiography showed extensive gas in the soft tissues (as shown in image). A Gram stain of the wound aspirate revealed only rare presence of neutrophils, and boxcar-shaped, gram positive rods. The organism most likely is:
questions.solutionHtml: ion of Incorrect Options: A. Staphylococcus aureus – Incorrect Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs), such as cellulitis, abscesses, and necrotizing fasciitis. However, it does not produce gas in tissues, and its Gram stain would show Gram-positive cocci in clusters, not boxcar-shaped rods. B. Enterococcus faecalis – Incorrect Enterococcus faecalis is an opportunistic pathogen associated with urinary tract infections (UTIs), endocarditis, and intra-abdominal infections, especially in hospitalized or immunocompromised patients. It is not a cause of gas gangrene, and its Gram stain would show Gram-positive cocci in pairs or chains, not rods. C. Streptococcus pyogenes – Incorrect Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) is a major cause of necrotizing fasciitis, a severe soft tissue infection that spreads rapidly and can be fatal. However, it does not produce gas in tissues, and its Gram stain would show Gram-positive cocci in chains, not boxcar-shaped rods.

questions.stem: A 14 year old boy in the village had gone for a swimming where he suffered a foot laceration while swimming in a polluted water area in a river. He did not seek medical treatment, and the wound developed a foul-smelling exudate. One of the bacteria isolated from the abscess exudate was missing superoxide dismutase, catalase, and a peroxidase. Which of the following statements best describes this microorganism?

options.label: C
options.text: It is a microaerophiled. It is an anaerobe

questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (D)

It is an anaerobe

The bacterium isolated from the foul-smelling abscess exudate in this case is most likely an obligate anaerobe, as it lacks superoxide dismutase, catalase, and peroxidase—enzymes that help bacteria detoxify reactive oxygen species (ROS). Anaerobic bacteria cannot survive in oxygen-rich environments because they are highly susceptible to oxidative damage.

The foul-smelling exudate suggests the presence of anaerobic bacteria, which produce volatile fatty acids and sulfur-containing compounds as metabolic byproducts, contributing to the characteristic odor. The contaminated river water and deep wound created an ideal anaerobic environment for such bacteria to thrive, leading to necrotic tissue and abscess formation.

Common anaerobic bacteria that could be involved include:

Clostridium species (e.g., C. perfringens – causes gas gangrene)
Bacteroides (e.g., B. fragilis – common in deep abscesses)
Fusobacterium and Peptostreptococcus
Incorrect Options:
(A) It is a capnophile – Incorrect. Capnophiles are bacteria that require increased carbon dioxide (CO2) levels for growth but can tolerate oxygen. Examples include Neisseria spp., Campylobacter spp., and Haemophilus spp. The bacterium in question lacks oxidative defense enzymes, meaning it is an obligate anaerobe, not a capnophile.

(B) It is a facultative anaerobe – Incorrect. Facultative anaerobes can grow in both the presence and absence of oxygen because they have superoxide dismutase and catalase, which protect them from oxidative stress. Examples include Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Salmonella spp. Since the isolated bacterium completely lacks these enzymes, it is an obligate anaerobe, not a facultative anaerobe.

(C) It is a microaerophile – Incorrect. Microaerophiles require low oxygen levels (2-10%) for survival and cannot grow in fully anaerobic conditions. They possess limited superoxide dismutase and catalase, allowing them to tolerate small amounts of oxygen. Examples include Helicobacter pylori and Campylobacter jejuni. The absence of oxidative defense enzymes in the isolated bacterium rules out microaerophilic bacteria.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl has been referred from a rural PHC to the district hospital with a sore throat, fever, malaise, and difficulty breathing. The girl has never been vaccinated. A gray membrane covering the pharynx is observed on physical examination. Corynebacterium diphtheriae is confirmed as the etiologic agent of this infection. Which of the following is required to prove that C. diphtheriae is the etiologic agent of this child’s infection?

options.label: B
options.text: Isolation of C. diphtheriae from throat culture

options.label: C
options.text: Metachromatic granules seen on methylene blue stain

options.label: D
options.text: Toxigenicity demonstrated by the Elek test

questions.answerText: Toxigenicity demonstrated by the Elek test
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Toxigenicity demonstrated by the Elek test The definitive diagnosis of diphtheria requires not just the isolation of Corynebacterium diphtheriae from the throat but also confirmation of toxin production, since only toxigenic strains cause clinical diphtheria. The Elek test is a specific immunodiffusion assay that detects the presence of diphtheria toxin by forming precipitin lines when the toxin reacts with antitoxin in an agar medium. This test is essential for confirming the pathogenic potential of the isolated bacteria. In this case, the unvaccinated child presents with a sore throat, fever, difficulty breathing, and a characteristic gray pseudomembrane, which are classic signs of diphtheria. However, since non-toxigenic C. diphtheriae strains exist, the Elek test is required to confirm toxigenicity, making (D) the correct answer. Incorrect Options: (A) Demonstration of cysteinase production – Incorrect. Cysteinase activity is used in biochemical identification of C. diphtheriae (e.g., in tellurite-containing media, C. diphtheriae forms black colonies due to tellurite reduction). However, this only confirms the presence of the bacterium, not its toxigenicity, which is the key factor in causing diphtheria symptoms. (B) Isolation of C. diphtheriae from throat culture – Incorrect. While culturing C. diphtheriae from the throat on selective media (Löffler's medium or tellurite agar) is important, not all strains of C. diphtheriae are toxigenic. Only toxin-producing strains cause diphtheria, so toxin production must be confirmed using the Elek test. (C) Metachromatic granules seen on methylene blue stain – Incorrect. Methylene blue staining shows metachromatic (volutin) granules, which are characteristic of Corynebacterium diphtheriae and help in presumptive identification. However, this does not confirm whether the strain is toxin-producing or not.

questions.stem: A 51 year old patient is hospitalized with complaint of sepsis developed in a surgical wound. The patient is treated with tobramycin, carbenicillin, and clindamycin. Five days after antibiotic therapy was initiated, the patient develops severe diarrhea and pseudomembranous enterocolitis. Pseudomembranous enterocolitis can be caused by which of the following organisms?
questions.solutionHtml: ion of the Correct Answer: The patient, who was hospitalized and treated with multiple antibiotics (tobramycin, carbenicillin, and clindamycin), developed severe diarrhea and pseudomembranous enterocolitis (PMC) five days after antibiotic therapy. This strongly suggests an infection with Clostridium difficile (C. difficile). C. difficile is a Gram-positive, spore-forming, anaerobic bacterium that is the most common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) and pseudomembranous colitis. Pathogenesis: Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt normal gut flora, allowing C. difficile overgrowth and toxin production. Toxin A (enterotoxin) increases intestinal permeability and inflammation, leading to diarrhea. Toxin B (cytotoxin) causes colonic epithelial damage, leading to pseudomembrane formation. Risk Factors: Recent antibiotic use (especially clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, and carbapenems) Hospitalization or long-term care facility stay Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), advanced age, and immunosuppression Clinical Features: Profuse, watery diarrhea Fever, leukocytosis, abdominal pain Pseudomembranous colitis, seen on colonoscopy as yellow-white plaques Diagnosis: Stool test for C. difficile toxins (PCR or ELISA for toxin A/B) Colonoscopy in severe cases shows pseudomembrane formation Treatment: First-line: Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin Alternative: Oral metronidazole for mild cases Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) for recurrent infections
